reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) directly contradicts the hypothesis's core premise: it states that tensile loading promotes clustering (not ordering) and that a clustering-to-ordering transition occurs only under high compressive strain, not tension. E3 concerns a different alloy and provides no support for the proposed mechanism in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
premises: High-strain-rate tensile loading of Al0.1CrCoFeNi induces a local chemical clustering and ordering transition.
This transition produces brittle nanodomains that act as crack nucleation sites.
The clustering/ordering transition causes a measurable loss in fracture toughness relative to the homogeneous baseline.
Compressive loading is expected to produce less clustering and a smaller toughness drop than tensile loading.
The proposed mechanism is specific to Al0.1CrCoFeNi under the stated service conditions.
